title: Rearrange Formulas

findings.finding: The opening topic does not rehearse inverse-operation equation solving before its worked example requires division by the complete coefficient Pr.
findings.breakdown: Following I = Prn to n = I/(Pr) requires students to recognise and undo the whole multiplicative coefficient. The statement about inverse operations does not check recall of this substantial prerequisite.
findings.checked: There is no opening review or preceding topic. p3-information states the principle, and p3-example-demonstration immediately applies it.
findings.assumptions: Basic numerical equation solving is prior knowledge, consistent with the course library. No calculator is required.

repair.proposal: Before p3-information, add: (a) Solve x+7=19. (b) Solve x−5=11. (c) Solve −4x=20. (d) Solve 3×5×x=60. (e) Solve x/6=8. Ask students to show the operation applied to both sides. Answers: 12, 16, −5, 4, 48. Keep the review within one page.

findings.doneWhen: The opening review checks inverse-operation choice and cancellation of a complete coefficient before the literal worked example.

findings.finding: Follow the two perimeter rearrangements with a numerical comparison of their equivalent expressions.
findings.breakdown: The follow-up connects the two existing methods and exposes why division applies to both terms of a difference.
findings.checked: For P=30 and l=6, both (P−2l)/2 and P/2−l give w=9. Distribution and both rearrangements are available within p7-q6.
findings.assumptions: Only the algebra already used in p7-q6 is required.

repair.proposal: After p7-q6-e, add: (f) For P=30 and l=6, find w using w=(P−2l)/2. Answer: 9. (g) For the same values, find w using w=P/2−l. Answer: 9. (h) Explain why the two formulas give the same result. Expected answer: Dividing both terms of P−2l by 2 gives P/2−l.

findings.doneWhen: The follow-up is attached to p7-q6 as separate parts with the stated expected answers.

findings.finding: The denominator topic does not rehearse subtraction of algebraic fractions before its third worked example uses it.
findings.breakdown: The transition from 1/f−1/u to (u−f)/(fu) requires choosing a common algebraic denominator and adjusting the numerators. Students must recall this substantial method while also learning the reciprocal rearrangement.
findings.checked: The earlier teaching does not rehearse combining algebraic fractions. p16-information-block explains denominator removal and reciprocation but does not explain the common-denominator step in p16-worked-3.
findings.assumptions: Algebraic fraction subtraction is prior knowledge, consistent with the separate Algebraic Fractions booklets. No calculator is required.

repair.proposal: Before p16-information-block, add: 'Write each expression as a single fraction. (a) 1/a−1/b; (b) 2/p−1/q; (c) 1/r−3/s.' Answers: (b−a)/(ab), (2q−p)/(pq), (s−3r)/(rs). Use nonzero denominators and keep the review within one page.

findings.doneWhen: The opening review checks common-denominator selection and subtraction of adjusted numerators before p16-worked-3.

findings.finding: The subject-appears-twice topic does not rehearse common-factor factorisation and literal bracket expansion before combining them in its examples.
findings.breakdown: Students must extract a common pronumeral, retain an implicit coefficient of 1, and distribute a literal multiplier. Naming factorisation does not check recall of these prerequisite steps.
findings.checked: p19-example-1-node and p19-example-2-node use common-factor extraction; p19-example-3-node combines literal expansion with factorisation of xy−x. Earlier numerical bracket expansion in p7-q6 does not rehearse this combination. The worked example brings together several earlier algebra methods, so the combined-method review exception applies.
findings.assumptions: Expansion and factorisation are prior knowledge, consistent with the separate course booklets. No calculator is required.

repair.proposal: Before p19-information-block, add: (a) Factorise ax+bx. (b) Factorise mx−nx. (c) Factorise xy−x. (d) Expand y(x+2). (e) Expand b(x−3). Answers: x(a+b), x(m−n), x(y−1), xy+2y, bx−3b. Keep the review within one page.

findings.doneWhen: The opening review checks common-factor extraction, including an implicit coefficient of 1, and distribution of a literal multiplier.

findings.finding: A numerical follow-up can connect the temperature conversion formula with equal Celsius and Fahrenheit readings.
findings.breakdown: Substituting F=C produces a numerical linear equation and gives a concrete reason to use the formula beyond direct conversion.
findings.checked: C=(9/5)C+32 gives −(4/5)C=32, so C=−40. Substitution confirms F=−40. The task uses the existing formula and prior numerical linear-equation solving.
findings.assumptions: Numerical linear-equation solving is prior knowledge, consistent with the course library.

repair.proposal: After p7-q5-b, add optional part c: 'At one temperature, the Fahrenheit reading and Celsius reading are the same number. Substitute F=C into F=(9/5)C+32 and find this temperature.' Expected answer: −40°C=−40°F.

findings.doneWhen: The optional follow-up is attached to p7-q5 and has the expected answer −40°C=−40°F.

findings.finding: The powers-and-roots teaching models the two-sign square-root rearrangement but does not explain the cube/cube-root variant used in practice.
findings.breakdown: At p11-q5-f, students must replace the modelled ± square root with a single cube root. At p11-q5-k, they must cube both sides. Applying the demonstrated square pattern mechanically can produce the wrong root index or an unnecessary ±.
findings.checked: p9-worked-r and p9-worked-M model only squares and square roots. The earlier teaching supplies basic inverse operations but no contrast between reversing squares and cubes. Later cube questions practise the distinction without explaining it.
findings.assumptions: Students recognise cube and cube-root notation. The missing teaching is the inverse choice and sign distinction in this rearrangement method. Calculator access does not resolve that choice.

repair.proposal: Before p11-q5-f, add: 'Cubing and taking a cube root undo each other. Unlike reversing a square, reversing a cube gives one real value: a³=T gives a=∛T, without ±. Conversely, ∛a=c gives a=c³.'

findings.doneWhen: Before the first cube task, students encounter both inverse directions and the explicit distinction from the ± square-root step.

findings.finding: A follow-up using p=12 can connect the ± notation with values that satisfy the original formulas.
findings.breakdown: Using the same input across the three existing formulas makes the effect of squaring visible numerically.
findings.checked: For p=12, parts a, b and c give q=4, q=±√8 and q=±2 respectively. Both signs in part c give p=2×4+4=12. All methods are available in this topic.
findings.assumptions: The pronumerals have no contextual restriction requiring q to be positive.

repair.proposal: After p10-q1-c, add optional parts: (d) 'When p=12, find q in part a.' Answer: 4. (e) 'When p=12, find both values of q in part b.' Answer: ±√8. (f) 'When p=12, find both values of q in part c.' Answer: ±2. (g) 'Explain why changing the sign of q leaves p unchanged in part c.' Answer: 2²=(−2)²=4, so both give p=12.

findings.doneWhen: The optional parts use the existing formulas and explicitly connect the two signs with substitution into the original equation.

dropped.reason: The shared-stem preceding part p4-q5-a already asks students to obtain F=AP. Dividing that equation by P, as modelled in p3-example-demonstration and p3-guided-d, gives A=F/P. The claim that students must independently discover a denominator-removal method is defeated by this existing scaffold.

candidates.finding: “Express A in terms of P and F” first places the requested subject in a denominator, although preceding teaching only isolates additive terms, factors and numerators.

dropped.reason: Earlier practice p4-q5-a–b already bridges numerator and denominator subjects through F=AP and A=F/P. Together with the two-step teaching, this supplies the operations needed for c=2b/a: ac=2b, then a=2b/c. A second denominator-subject model is not a missing prerequisite.

candidates.finding: The row containing c=2b/a asks students to make a the subject, introducing a subject in the denominator without modelling that variant.
